nitwit.e: First attested in the 1910s in the US Northeast. Likely from German nit, dialect form of nichts (“nothing”), or Yiddish ניט (nit), dialect form of נישט (nisht, “no”), although some dictionaries give the alternative etymology nit (“louse egg; something very small”) + wit.

s.d: a stupid incompetent person
(informal) A scatterbrained or stupid person.
x: If you don't remember you are a nitwit. If you do answer, well, you know what the penalty is for perjury.
"Don't be a nitwit, honey!" says Adele. "Here, let me open the door! Ma be I did leave them lights on, though it ain't ike me!"

s.d: (of especially persons) lacking sense or understanding or judgment
(informal) Being like a nitwit; being foolish or stupid.
x: Fifty thousand pounds our esteemed father-in-law was proposing to settle upon that half-baked, nitwitted little slypuss.

nix.e: From German nix, colloquial form of nichts (“nothing”). Compare also Dutch niks (“nothing”), informal for niets (“nothing”). More at naught.

s.d: a quantity of no importance; thing (object:), singular, negative pronoun; pronoun, thing, singular; quantifier: negative existential
x: it looked like nothing I had ever seen before
reduced to nil all the work we had done

s.d: (colloquial, uncountable) Nothing.
A treacherous water-spirit
x: A girl from a village near Lei[zig was one time at service in the house of a Nix.

s.d: command against
x: I forbid you to call me late at night
Mother vetoed the trip to the chocolate store

s.d: To make something become nothing; to reject or cancel.
x: Nix the last order – the customer walked out.
Sticks Nix Hick Pix [headline]

s.d: To destroy or eradicate.
No! Not at all!
x: "Ugh! An inventor, eh?" "Nix! He's not an inventor himself, but he antes-up for 'em."

s.d: (obsolete) A warning cry when a policeman or schoolmaster etc. was seen approaching.
